title: Orientation with shortest round trip
exact_target:
Can one efficiently orient the undirected edges of a mixed graph
to minimize the combined shortest outward and return distances between two vertices?
definition_tex:
\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
A finite mixed graph consists of vertices $V$, fixed directed arcs
$A$, and undirected edges $E$. Each edge and arc has a nonnegative
rational length. An orientation selects a direction for every member
of $E$ and leaves every arc in $A$ unchanged. For a resulting digraph
$D$, let $d_D(u,v)$ be the length of a shortest directed path, with
value $\infty$ if no such path exists.

Given distinct vertices $s,t$, can one compute in polynomial time
an orientation minimizing
\[
                                d_D(s,t)+d_D(t,s),
\]
or determine that no orientation permits travel in both directions?
Polynomial time is measured against the graph description and binary
encoding of the lengths. An optimum orientation and two realizing
paths provide a concrete output.

Each undirected edge receives one permanent direction, not a separate
direction for the outward and return trips. The two paths may share
vertices and may reuse a fixed arc in the same direction; no additional
disjointness condition is imposed. Shortest-path distances in the
original mixed graph, obtained by temporarily allowing an undirected
edge both ways, need not be simultaneously realizable after orientation.
The objective minimizes their sum, rather than requiring either trip
to retain its individually best possible length. The fixed directed
arcs distinguish this problem from orienting a wholly undirected graph.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Can one efficiently orient the undirected edges of a mixed graph
to minimize the combined shortest outward and return distances between two vertices?
